content: The GUSTO-I trial, formally known as the Global Utilization of Streptokinase and t-PA for Occluded Coronary Arteries I Trial, enrolled 41,021 patients who presented with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and ST-segment elevation within six hours of symptom onset. Patients were randomized into one of four thrombolytic treatment strategies. Importantly, there were no restrictions on enrollment based on age or the presence of cardiogenic shock. However, patients were excluded if they had a history of prior stroke, active or recent bleeding, recent trauma or major surgery, non-compressible vascular punctures, or prior treatment with streptokinase or anistreplase. The four treatment regimens were as follows: 1. Streptokinase with subcutaneous heparin: Patients received 1.5 million units of streptokinase infused over one hour, followed by subcutaneous heparin (12,500 units twice daily) starting four hours after the streptokinase infusion. 2. Streptokinase with intravenous heparin: Patients received the same dose of streptokinase (1.5 million units over one hour) but were given intravenous heparin instead. This began with a 5,000-unit bolus, followed by a continuous infusion of 1,000 units per hour, adjusted to maintain an activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) of 60 to 85 seconds. 3. Accelerated t-PA (tissue plasminogen activator): Patients received a 15 mg bolus of t-PA, followed by an infusion of 0.75 mg/kg over 30 minutes (up to a maximum of 50 mg) and then 0.5 mg/kg over the next hour (up to a maximum of 35 mg). This was combined with the same intravenous heparin regimen as described above. 4. Combination therapy with t-PA and streptokinase: Patients received t-PA at a dose of 1 mg/kg over one hour (up to a maximum of 90 mg, with 10% given as a bolus) and streptokinase at a dose of 1 million units over one hour, administered simultaneously through separate intravenous cannulas. This was also combined with the same intravenous heparin regimen. The primary endpoint of the study was all-cause mortality at 30 days. Mortality data for hospitalized patients were recorded on the main case report form, while post-discharge mortality data were collected via return postcards or telephone follow-up. Mortality status at 30 days was available for 40,946 patients (99.8% of the cohort). Additionally, one-year follow-up data were obtained for 39,119 patients (95.3% of the cohort). Secondary endpoints included the occurrence of stroke, a composite of death or stroke, and a composite of death or nonfatal, disabling stroke. Neurological deficits that were fatal or persisted for at least 24 hours were reviewed by an independent, blinded committee. Strokes were classified into four categories: primary intracranial hemorrhage, non-hemorrhagic infarction, hemorrhagic conversion of infarction, and unknown. Anatomic or diagnostic confirmation of stroke was achieved in 93% of cases. Bleeding complications were categorized as severe or life-threatening if they were intracranial or caused hemodynamic compromise requiring intervention. Moderate bleeding was defined as bleeding that necessitated a blood transfusion. To analyze the relationship between age and clinical outcomes, patients were divided into four age groups: <65 years, 65–74 years, 75–84 years, and ≥85 years. Discrete variables were summarized using frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were described using means ± standard deviations (SDs) or medians with interquartile ranges (25th and 75th percentiles). Clinical outcomes were tabulated by both age group and treatment assignment. Kaplan-Meier estimates were used to calculate mortality rates at 24 hours, 30 days, and one year, allowing for the visualization of treatment effects across different age groups. Ordinary least-squares regression was employed to assess the statistical significance of relationships between age and baseline characteristics. Logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between age and 30-day outcomes, while Cox proportional hazards modeling was applied to assess the relationship between age and one-year mortality. Cubic spline functions were utilized to evaluate the shapes of these relationships in both mortality models.
